text:
This is a dollar bill. It costs about four cents to make. And almost everything you were taught about it… is wrong.

...

This is Jake. And this is Ryan. They grew up on the same street. Same school. Same grades. At 25, they even start at the same company. Same job. Same salary.

...

Twenty years later…

...

…one of them is a millionaire. The other one is still renting, and still in debt. Ryan isn't smarter. He didn't win the lottery. He didn't get lucky. He just learned something Jake never did: how money really works. What the banks know. What the rich know. And in the next 15 minutes, you're going to learn it too.

chap: 1:45 – SECRET #1: YOUR MONEY ISN'T IN THE BANK
text:
It starts with Jake's first paycheck. He puts it in the bank. Safe. Exactly where you're supposed to. At least, that's what he thinks.

...

Here's the first thing nobody tells you: The moment you deposit money, it stops being yours… in the way you think. Legally, you've just lent your money to the bank. Your balance isn't a pile of cash with your name on it. It's a promise. The bank owes you.

...

And the bank doesn't keep your money lying around. It uses it. Lends it. Invests it.

...

While Jake sleeps, his paycheck is already working, for the bank. It might be financing a stranger's car at seven or eight percent interest. Jake gets almost nothing for it. The bank keeps the difference. And Jake? He doesn't even know it's gone. His app still shows $5,000. Because the app doesn't show the money. It shows the promise. For decades, American banks at least had to keep a small part of their deposits in reserve. In March 2020, that requirement was lowered to zero. Zero percent.

...

So how much money is actually sitting in the vault, waiting for Jake? Far less than he thinks. But that's not even the strangest part. Because the bank doesn't just lend out Jake's money. It can create money that never existed.

chap: 3:30 – SECRET #2: BANKS CREATE MONEY OUT OF NOTHING
text:
A few years later, Ryan buys his first house. He takes out a 300,000-dollar mortgage. Most people imagine the bank opens its vault, takes 300,000 dollars that other customers saved, and hands it over. That's not what happens.

...

The bank types 300,000 dollars into existence. One second, the money doesn't exist. The next second, it does. This isn't a conspiracy theory. The Bank of England, one of the oldest central banks in the world, said it in plain language in 2014: The majority of money in the modern economy is created by commercial banks… making loans.

...

And it works in reverse. Every month, when Ryan pays back his mortgage, that money doesn't go back into a vault. It's deleted.

...

Think about what this means. Almost every dollar in the system was born as somebody's debt. If everyone paid back every debt tomorrow, most of the money in the world would simply disappear. Money is debt.

...

By the end of 2025, American households owed about 18.8 trillion dollars. Mortgages. Car loans. Student loans. Credit cards. And now look at Ryan's mortgage from the bank's side.

...

300,000 dollars, over 30 years, at seven percent interest. By the time Ryan has paid it off, he'll have paid the bank about 718,000 dollars. More than 400,000 of that is just interest.

...

Let that sink in. The bank created the 300,000 dollars out of nothing… and will collect more than 400,000 dollars in interest for it. And if money is debt… then someone is making a fortune from all that debt. Want to guess who else?

chap: 5:30 – SECRET #3: HOW THE BANK MAKES MONEY ON YOU
text:
Let's look at Jake's money from the bank's side. Jake keeps his savings in a regular savings account. For that, many big banks pay him a tiny interest rate. Often well under one percent. At the same time, Jake carries a balance on his credit card. In 2025, the average credit card interest rate in America was around 21 percent.

...

So the bank borrows Jake's money for almost nothing… and lends money back to people like Jake for twenty times more. That gap is one of the oldest business models on Earth.

...

And the card companies have a favorite trick: the minimum payment. Say Jake owes 5,000 dollars at 21 percent, and only pays the minimum each month. It can take him around 19 years to pay it off. And he'll pay roughly 7,700 dollars in interest. More than the original debt.

...

And if you think that's bad, the price of money gets even worse the poorer you are. A typical payday loan charges 15 dollars for every 100 dollars borrowed, for just two weeks. According to America's consumer protection agency, that works out to an annual rate of almost 400 percent. But there's another one most people never notice.

...

Every time you pay with a card, the store pays a fee. Often around two percent. In 2024, American businesses paid about 187 billion dollars in card fees. And where do you think stores get that money?

...

From you. It's built into the prices. Even when you pay cash, you pay for everyone's cards. The bank makes money when you save. It makes money when you borrow. It makes money when you shop. But the biggest money machine of all isn't a bank. It's the place where new money is born.

chap: 8:00 – SECRET #4: THE LEAK – WHO GETS NEW MONEY FIRST
text:
This is the Federal Reserve, America's central bank. When there's a crisis, the Fed can create money on a scale no normal bank ever could. No printing press needed. It buys bonds from banks and pays with money it creates on a computer.

...

Before the 2008 financial crisis, everything the Fed owned was worth under 900 billion dollars. By 2022, it was almost 9 trillion. Ten times more. When the pandemic hit, it jumped in just one year from about 4.2 trillion to more than 7.5 trillion.

...

If you spent a million dollars every single day, it would take you more than 20,000 years to spend 8 trillion. So where did all that money go? Here's the part that changes how you see everything.

...

New money doesn't arrive everywhere at once. It enters at the top. Through banks. Through financial markets. The people closest to it get it first, and they spend it before prices rise. Everyone else gets it last. Economists call this the Cantillon effect, named after an 18th-century banker who noticed it 300 years ago. And in 2020, you could watch it happen live.

...

American home prices rose more than 30 percent in just two years. The stock market doubled from its 2020 low in under 18 months. People who owned houses and stocks… like Ryan… got richer without doing anything.

...

Ryan's 300,000-dollar house was suddenly worth around 390,000. He gained about 90,000 dollars in two years, while sleeping. More than his salary for an entire year.

...

People who owned nothing… like Jake… just watched everything become more expensive. Same salary. Same street. Completely different result. And there's one more force quietly working against Jake, every single day. One he never agreed to.

In 1971, 100 dollars could fill a cart like this. Today, to buy the same things, you need about 800 dollars.

...

Nobody stole your money. It's still the same bill. It just buys less. Every year. That's inflation. And here's what most people never hear: It's not an accident.

...

The Federal Reserve officially aims for prices to rise by about two percent every year. Two percent sounds small. But over 35 years, two percent a year cuts what your money can buy in half.

...

So Jake, saving responsibly in his bank account at under one percent… is actually getting poorer every year. Slowly. Quietly.

...

Let's say Jake has saved 20,000 dollars, earning half a percent. If prices rise by three percent that year, his savings lose around 500 dollars in real value. In one year. Without him spending a single cent. Do that for ten years, and Jake has worked months of his life for money that simply melted away. And Ryan? His house and his stocks tend to rise with prices. Inflation melts cash. And it rewards people who own things. Which brings us to the question you've been waiting for: How do the really rich play this game?

chap: 12:00 – SECRET #6: HOW THE RICH PLAY THE GAME
text:
Jake earns money, pays tax on it, and saves what's left. Ryan earns money and buys assets. But the richest people on Earth go one step further. They barely use income at all.

...

Their wealth sits in shares of their companies. And shares that aren't sold aren't taxed. So when they need money for a house, a jet, a new company… they don't sell.

...

They borrow. Using their shares as collateral. A loan isn't income. So it isn't taxed like income. The shares keep growing. The loans get paid with new loans.

...

Imagine someone with one billion dollars in shares. If those shares grow eight percent in a year, that's 80 million dollars of new wealth. They borrow 10 million to live on. At five percent, the interest is 500,000 dollars. No salary. No sale. And no income tax on the 10 million. The wealth keeps growing faster than the debt. And when they die?

...

Under American tax law, their heirs inherit those shares at today's value. All the gains that built up over a lifetime are never taxed as capital gains. In finance, this has a dark nickname: Buy. Borrow. Die.

...

In 2021, the newsroom ProPublica got hold of secret IRS data. They compared what the 25 richest Americans paid in taxes to how much their wealth grew. Between 2014 and 2018, that was what ProPublica called a "true tax rate" of just 3.4 percent.

...

It's legal. It's just a different game. And it all runs on one thing Jake has been taught to fear: debt.

Here's the cruelest part of the whole system. Money has a price. It's called interest. And the price is not the same for everyone. Jake pays around 21 percent on his credit card. The billionaire, borrowing against millions in shares, can often borrow for a fraction of that.

...

The less money you have, the more money costs you. The more money you have, the cheaper money gets. And look at what each one borrows for. Jake borrows to buy things that lose value. A TV. A car. A vacation. The rich borrow to buy things that gain value. Companies. Buildings. Shares. For most people, debt is a trap. For the people who understand money, debt is a tool. Same thing. Opposite result. But what happens when the people playing with all this debt get it wrong?

chap: 15:15 – SECRET #8: HEADS THEY WIN, TAILS YOU LOSE
text:
March 9th, 2023. Silicon Valley Bank, one of the biggest banks in America. A rumor spreads. Group chats explode. "Get your money out."

...

In a single day, customers tried to withdraw 42 billion dollars. But remember Secret Number One. The money was never all there.

...

The next morning, regulators shut the bank down. In America, deposits are only insured up to 250,000 dollars. Most of the money at this bank was above that limit. And yet, two days later, the government guaranteed every single dollar. Even above the limit. Why? Because if trust breaks at one bank, people start running from the next.

...

We've seen this before. In 2008, when the big banks gambled and lost, Congress approved a 700-billion-dollar rescue program.

...

And a few months later, the insurance giant AIG, which had just been rescued with taxpayer money, paid out around 165 million dollars in bonuses to its employees. According to New York's attorney general, 73 of them received at least one million dollars each.

...

When the system wins, the profits are private. When it loses, the losses become everyone's problem. Heads, they win. Tails… you lose.

chap: 16:45 – FINALE: THE DOLLAR ON THE TABLE
text:
So let's go back to Jake and Ryan. Same street. Same school. Same salary. Jake did everything he was told. He saved cash. He borrowed for things. He trusted the bank to keep his money. Ryan learned the rules. Cash loses value. So he owned things. New money flows to assets first. So he owned assets. Debt is a tool. So he only used it to buy things that grow.

...

And here's the part that hurts the most. If Jake had simply put 300 dollars a month into a broad stock market fund from age 25, and it had grown at the market's long-term average of around ten percent a year, which is never guaranteed, by 45 he would have had around 228,000 dollars. From just 72,000 dollars of his own money. The rest? The same force the rich use every day. Owning things that grow. Neither of them did anything illegal. Neither of them was smarter. The only difference was knowing how money really works.

...

Look at that dollar again. Four cents of paper. Most money like it was never printed. Only typed into existence, the moment someone took on debt. And it's worth a little less every year. It works for one reason only: we all keep believing in it.

...

Now you know the rules. Most people never will.

...

If this changed how you see money, subscribe. There's a lot more the banks will never tell you.
